Sweden Unlocked: A Unique Approach to Combating Covid

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As lockdowns and their inevitable economic toll take hold across the globe, Sweden is cutting against the grain by staying open for business and relying on citizens to do the right thing.

Unique Selling Point:
If lockdowns constitute a global experiment, Sweden is the control group. While the vast majority of states have chosen extreme caution as the best means to combat Covid19 - sacrificing their economies in the process -Sweden has opted for a different path. They haven't insisted on businesses shutting down, they've kept schools and universities open, and public transport has operated as normal. Their most powerful weapon is a responsible citizenry, they say; people who'll keep a social distance because it's the right thing to do.

Controversially, many of Sweden's epidemiologists have argued for herd immunity, believing a 60% infection rate will achieve that. They also claim the virus has infected a lot more people than current estimates suggest and that immunity is closer as a result. One of their most outspoken medical scientists has criticised countries like the U.K. for abandoning herd immunity and over-estimating the cost of the virus to human life. It's not a popular position in many quarters - not even in Sweden - but is routinely used by lockdown critics around the world as an example for other countries to follow. Most recently, and surprisingly, Sweden was hailed as a shining light by the WHO.

A locally-based crew will film on the streets of Stockholm where life - while far from normal - is continuing lockdown-free. They'll also talk to experts on both sides of the debate, including the country's chief epidemiologist, a hospital clinician working with Covid patients, Sweden's foreign minister and a Swede who is infected with Covid19 and has been for the past 40-odd days.

It'll be a first-hand look at the country everyone is talking about. It'll also offer an insight into an issue that is far more complex than many people realise - including those arguing against the lockdown in South Africa.

Summary:
This is the story of a country that has followed its own path in the battle against Covid19. It's relied on a responsible public to do the right thing in helping keeping Sweden open for business. As a result, the pandemic has come at less of a price for Swedes than it has for others. But, it's not without controversy: the death rate is the highest in Scandinavia and there are ongoing warnings of a health system that risks being overwhelmed. But, the Swedes remain resolute that theirs has been the correct approach and that others - South Africa included - have got it wrong.

The story will be told through the eyes of Swedish journalist, Marika Griehsel as she ventures through the streets of Stockholm. It's quieter than usual, but notably busier than most other cities around the world. She'll talk to experts and those on the frontline and, as a personal insight, visit the nursing home where her father is being cared for. She's not aloud inside and has to stand in the street and shout to him at his third-floor window. The vulnerable are isolated, the rest of society goes about daily life as best it can.

Further information:
One of the upsides of this piece is that in-person filming is still possible, so the insert will be Skype/Zoom free.

As an interesting twist, the Swedes don't wear masks. Another sign that this is a country with its own take on the science and a determination to do things its own way.

Script:


VO:
Tucked away between Norway and Finland, my home country, Sweden, has always quietly gone about its business.
Now as the world battles the deadly coronavirus pandemic, its strategy, is receiving a lot of attention from international scientists and governments alike.

Here Swedish authorities are taking the road less travelled – they’re not enforcing a national lockdown – and they’re simply trusting citizens to protect each other against the virus.

But emergency physician, Katrin Ruske was one of the first to question the preparedness of the country’s public health system.

Katrin Ruske ( Emergency Doctor ):
This outbreak is a disaster for everyone in the world and when I realised that, many weeks ago, that this was going to happen to us, there was no way I could stop it and there was no way anyone else could stop it either I just broke down and cried then called my brother whose also a doctor and said. They’re just going to let this happen and we’re going to get infected and people are going to die and I can only do my best to take care of my patients the best I can and not be overwhelmed by this whole chaos that is going on in society.

VO:
At a daily press briefing, state epidemiologist, Anders Tegnell presents grim statistics. 37 deaths per hundred thousand puts Sweden among the five most badly affected countries in the world.
Tegnell and his team however don’t seem fazed by the numbers. continue to express their belief in the strategy that they have created.

Dr. Anders Tegnell (Swedish State Epidemiologist ):
I think it’s very important to build trust with your population. To really get your population involved in whatever you are doing and getting an understanding in your population for what is needed to be done. So they can look at their situation and see how they can keep social distancing and so on working where they live and where they act.

VO:
Professor Johan Giesecke, senior advisor to the world health organisation, is an outspoken critic of a hard lockdown.


Professor. Johan Giesecke ( Senior advisor to WHO):
I call it a soft lockdown because it seems like many people in the world and many media think we are doing nothing to prevent the spread of COVID which is of course not true. We are doing a lot of things. The main difference is that most measures are voluntary. There are very few laws or ordinances about how people can behave. We said early that we will not take any measure that does not have a scientific foundation.

Vox Pop teenage girls on camera.

Couple cross street towards camera.

Vox Pop adult man on camera

Vox Pop elderly couple
On camera

VO:
And soft it might appear. As spring makes its way back people are out enjoying the sunshine, shops and restaurants are open and some commuters are off to work. people are still commuting to work. The only restrictions here prevent gatherings of more than 50 people, isolate old age homes and senior schools and universities are closed.
But despite staying open, Sweden’s export driven economy is still predicted to shrink by 6%, slightly less than more restrictive European countries.


Vox Pop 1 teenage girls:
We can’t really meet our grandparents but otherwise its not such a big deal for us. Our school is still open so that’s good.

Vox Pop 2:
I have to say that in Sweden we have carried on. I think we’ve been quite respectful of keeping distance but friendship-wise and social life-wise we’ve all been hanging out and doing things but still within reason, yeah!

Vox Pop 3:
We trust ourselves, so.
We’re trying …. as good as we can.
Sometime life will end anyway, anyhow….Laughs.

VO: to camera:
So this means keep your distance “ Hål avstånd “.
And I can still go to my favourite bakery as long as I comply.

Of course after you have used a machine. You clean your hands.
VO:
The Swedish government support package now stands at a record high 450 billion rand. It is an important pillar of the countries broad based public health, social and economic mitigation strategy.

Ann Linde ( Foreign Minister )
We don’t believe in locking people in their homes.
It’s for healthcare reasons, its to mitigate the possibility of domestic violence.
The Authority said that there is not a lot of spreading among children and youth. If we close the schools one parent has to stay home. That will have great effect on the economy, on the healthcare sector, on the elderly care sector if you have to keep so many grown up people at home taking care of children.

Professor. Johan Giesecke:
To keep a hard lockdown is very costly. It needs a lot of people to check that other people are doing the right thing, that’s one and it’s fascinating that you install these lockdown measures but no country in Europe that I know of has given a second thought to how do we get out of this again. Everyone in the world will be exposed and most people will be infected if we don’t get a vaccine or a cure and this will take time and I’m not sure we have that much time.

VO:
It remains to be seen whether Sweden’s strategy will spare it from a second wave of infection and some experts predict that Sweden could lose anything from between six to 14 thousand people could die from COVID-19.

At a makeshift factory volunteers, many of whom are now jobless due to the pandemic, produce plastic aprons for a healthcare system that is overwhelmed.

Soraya Hashim. Social entrepreneur.
For a lot of people this is a sense of control in very confusing times because we’ve always trusted that the functions in Swedish society work and we kind of, I don’t know. That feeling of confusion now when it doesn’t work, when we didn’t have the safety net that we thought we had. I think it’s a bit helpful to do something with your hands, to be here and help to do …something real

Leyla Hakal. Friend to A Covid 19 victim:
I saw yesterday that people were coming here to put flowers for other people that are just numbers in the statistics and I thought, my friend is not a number in the statistics so I want to put these flowers for him.
They found that he had corona and he was at home sick and he died alone in his bed. For me it got so close, the corona virus, when my friend died so I got so scared.

Marika VO to camera:
So I’m here to see Anya she’s been sick for more than 50 days. She hasn’t had a test but all the symptoms are as if she has Covid 19 and I brought the Swedish Fika ( Coffee & Cakes ) basket.

Marika: No fever today?
Anya: No, not yet.
VO: Widespread testing isn’t yet available, so infection and immunity statistics, are at best, still just an estimate.

Anya L. Sundberg ( journalist ):
After a few weeks the lungs started hurting and I got this weird feeling of wearing a corset made of iron or something. I just wanted to take it off. And then when the lungs got better a few weeks after that then the blood vessels started hurting in really weird way. I actually tried to draw it here… These are the different sort of pain attacks that I got.
So people don’t really understand that this is killing people all over the world and it’s killing people like me not just elderly people and sick people, even though their lives are as much worth as mine. People should really understand.

VO:
What we know so far is that 80% of those who have died in Sweden are over 70 years old and the majority of them lived in some kind of care facility. A major setback and a matter of grave concern for Tegnell and his team.

Anders Tegnell:
I think what our society needs to become better at is protecting the very old in our population because they are the ones that are suffering the most.

Marika VO to camera:
I’m on my way to visit my father, he’s 92 and his old age home has been closed since mid-march and the closest I can get to him now is to wave from the street.

VO:
I meet up with my sister, Helena. She’s a nurse with insight into the challenging working conditions at many of Sweden’s old age homes. Staff here are often hired on an hourly basis, so when they get ill or have mild symptoms, it makes it difficult for them to stay at home and isolate.

Helena Griehsel ( Nursing sister )
I’m very worried because we know that the corona virus has hit this old age home like so many other old age homes in Sweden.

Music … hymn. ( You know that you are valued )

VO:
A local church choir relieves the monotony of lockdown at my father’s old age home. A welcome distraction... but regardless of whichever strategy a country chooses – the outcomes are far from certain.

Katrin Ruske:
Everything is so normal that it’s surreal and most people don’t see the sick patients. Even though they say that most of us have been infected most people don’t know someone who has been in infected and who has been severely ill in this disease and still people are just expected to accept all these regulations and all the restrictions to their ordinary lives. I have a very deep respect that this is very difficult for all of us to accept.

Music up:

Church choir live.
